page.title: Build a team chat, step by step
page.description: Build a team chat with tinyactors in five steps: rooms, presence, a workspace, a status roster, and a thousand users with fifty in memory.

hero.headline: Build a team chat, step by step.
hero.lede: A team chat is a system of things with lifecycles: workspaces that make rooms, rooms that fan out posts, people who connect, go idle and leave. This tutorial builds one in five steps. Each step is a program you can run, and each adds one idea to the step before. By the end, a thousand users run with fifty of them in memory.

section.heading: A room is an actor.
section.p: A room keeps a list of members. Your program sends it events, and it sends each post out. Its chart has one state. A join adds a member, and a post sends the message to an I/O processor of type chat:client:
The program gives the host that processor: an object with receive(send), standing in for the users' screens. Then it starts one room and sends it three events.
The room does no I/O. It decides who gets a message, and your program delivers it.

section.heading: People come and go.
section.p: Each user is now an actor too, offline, active or away. online holds active and away, so one disconnect leaves either. An active user turns away after 300 seconds without activity: entering active sends the actor an idle event, delayed, and activity cancels it and starts it again.

The room no longer talks to your program. It sends each post to each member's user actor, by name, and a user shows a message only while it is online. An offline user has no transition for message, so the event is dropped.
The program runs on a SimulatedClock, so 300 seconds take no time:

section.heading: The workspace makes the rooms.
section.p: In step 2 your program spawned the room. Now a workspace actor decides which rooms exist, and it alone spawns them. It sends a request to the package's Spawner, an I/O processor that spawns actors, and remembers who asked under the request's send id. The Spawner answers spawned with that id. A second request for one name finds it in rooms or in creating, so no room is made twice.
The user actor now joins rooms and posts to them, by name. A send to a name no actor has fails at once: the sender gets error.communication with the send's id, and tells its screen.
Your program asks the workspace with actor.ask. The workspace answers to _event.origin, and ask returns the answer.

section.heading: Everyone sees who is here.
section.p: The workspace now keeps a roster of each user's status. Each state of a user reports itself to the workspace on entry, so a status is sent only when it changes. A user who comes online gets the whole roster, and the other online users get each change.
cameOnline and online are functions of the chart's <script>, which take the variables they read as arguments.

section.heading: A thousand users, fifty in memory.
section.p: Most users and rooms wait most of the time, so the host can keep them out of memory. The charts do not change in this step, only the host's options. resident is the most actors the host keeps in memory: after each turn it hibernates the rest into store, an object with save, load and delete.

An event for a hibernated actor wakes it: the host loads its blob, deletes it from the store and delivers the event. A user's idle timer stays in the host while the user is out of memory, and wakes the user when it is due. Your program never wakes an actor itself. The post reached a hundred users, most of them in the store, and the bound held throughout.
This store keeps the blobs in a Map. The package has MemoryStore, and SQLiteStore for blobs that outlive the process.

section.heading: From here to production.
section.p: The charts stay as they are. What changes is what your program connects them to.

item.text: The chat:client processor writes to each user's socket instead of a list, and a socket's close sends disconnect.
SQLiteStore keeps hibernated users and rooms on disk, and a snapshot keeps the whole host.
Add a new version of the user chart: new users start in it, and a migration moves the running ones while messages keep coming.
Every step an actor takes is a span, so a slow post shows which room and which users it went through.
